recommendations.text: To require the Czech authorities: to take corrective measures as regards observed deficiencies in particular the Czech approval procedure for meat product export establishments and its implementation, and to approve the establishments for export to the Member States of the Community accordingly;

To list the Czech meat product establishments proposed by the Czech authorities on the basis of the above mentioned;

Resources should be used first of all to improve working conditions in the laboratories and district departments. Every laboratory must have basic equipment. It is absolutely essential to purchase equipment, in particular for laboratories. Where resources are limited, these should be targeted, i.e. a reduction in the number of laboratories should be considered.
Technical training of staff should be carried out only if the laboratories are suitably equipped.
Training in general management/administrative tasks should also be given alongside technical training.
A register of persons and firms subject to phytosanitary instructions is urgently required. This is the only way of guaranteeing that the whole system is monitored by the SPA's inspectors.

Since the majority of border inspection points will no longer be necessary once the Czech Republic becomes a member of the EU, PHARE resources should no longer be used for this purpose, particularly since the border inspection points inspected are operational. 5

It is also recommended that the Czech Republic should make more efficient use of the border inspection points, e.g. by modifying working hours, transferring inspections of exports to district level and abandoning duplicate inspections, carrying out inspections on demand (which is the practice in the Member States) and making inspectors responsible for managing the respective districts.
It is necessary to amend those sections of the legislation relating to the fitting out of border inspection points, in particular with laboratories. 6

audits.title: evaluate the traceability of animal by-products (ABP) and derived products

recommendations.text: To ensure that all operators active in the ABP chain, notably paper traders and carriers of ABP/DP are subject to official controls, as required by Article 45 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009.

citations.text: No systematic controls of transporters are in place and while random checks on transporters are carried out at the place of origin and at the place of destination of ABP/DP, these checks focus on the presence of commercial documents and the registration status of transporters. According to the SVA representatives, transporters are informed about their duties at registration. 5 a) The first road haulier visited involved in transport of Category 1 fat, had been informed by the regional veterinary inspectors of the relevant legal requirements at the time of his application for registration. The operator held a register of all commercial documents for the previous two years as this had been required by the regional inspectors. Although the operator was not subject to official controls, the audit team saw evidence that this particular haulier had been controlled at a technical plant visited. Moreover, all inspectors met during the audit declared that they check the registration status of transporters and the completeness of commercial documents at the place of origin or at the place of destination. b) At the second transporter visited, involved in transport of Category 3 dairy products, the audit team confirmed that the operator had received information concerning his legal obligations regarding traceability requirements. Moreover, the regional inspectors provided evidence that traceability requirements had been checked at the place of loading. The audit team noted that the operator kept a register of the commercial documents as required by EU legislation.

Although the audit team noticed a satisfactory level of compliance as regards the registration status of transporters and their compliance with the requirements for commercial documents, the absence of regular official controls for carriers transporting certain types of ABP/DP is not in line with the requirements laid down in Article 45 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009.

According to SVA, paper traders of ABP/DP are not subject to regular official controls as required by article 45 to Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009, because they may be difficult to locate and, in some cases, they are shown on the commercial documents as receivers or dispatchers of derived products for reasons of commercial confidentiality, although the products are never held on their premises (in most cases there are no premises where ABP/DP could be kept). The audit team noted the following: a) At one rendering plant visited, approximately 2.250 tonnes of Category 2 MBM were sold to a non-registered paper trader in 2013. The final destination given in the commercial documents was the office of this trader which lacked the storage facilities needed if this were the actual physical destination of the consignments. In the same way, additional consignments of Category 2 MBM declared as OF/SI had also been sent to this paper trader from another rendering plant. Official controls at the rendering plants from which these consignments were dispatched had not identified these issues. Additional information provided to the SVA following a traceability exercise indicated an office to be the final destination of approximately 1,900 tonnes of Category 2 MBM sold by a rendering plant to a non-registered trader in the Czech Republic. Only approximately 20% of the consignments of ABP shown in TRACES as arriving at the rendering plant in 2013 and 2014 had been confirmed as required. b) At a second rendering plant visited, the audit team compared the commercial documents and the TRACES notifications of two consignments of ruminant PAP. According to the commercial documents prepared by the rendering plant, the place of destination for these consignments was a registered paper trader. However, the TRACES notifications (drawn up by the trader) gave a destination in another Member State. According to data extracted from TRACES, the trader concerned had received approximately 580 such consignments in 2013 and no confirmation checks were encoded in TRACES for that year. Data extracted from TRACES for the first nine months of 2014, showed that approximately 170 out of 900 consignments were checked at this trader. 6

Adequate arrangements are in place to enable the organisation and planning of regular official controls to monitor and verify that most operators comply with the requirements relating to the traceability of ABP/DP. However, the fact that paper traders and carriers transporting ABP/DP by road are not subject to regular official controls as required, limits the ability of the competent authorities to ensure the traceability of ABP/DP handled by these operators.

responses.response: SVA: Information from the DG(SANCO) mission, as well as the findings/conclusions of the FVO inspectors concerning the duties of the carriers of and traders in the ABP/DP, and the supervision on such activities, were communicated and subsequently discussed within the meeting held on 12 November 2014. Based on remarks, the minimum frequency of checks on establishments handling ABP/DP was altered within the Uniform integrate multiannual national control plan for the year 2015. Checks on the carriers of and traders in the ABP/DP were included in the plan.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the arrival in the Czech Republic of all consignments of products referred to in Article 48(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 is notified via TRACES.

citations.text: According to data extracted from TRACES for 2013 by the audit team, approximately 3.600 commercial document notifications were sent to the Czech Republic from several Member States and the arrival of around 860 (24%) of these consignments was confirmed. Approximately 90% of these confirmations (770 out of 860) concerned Category 1 fat arriving at two technical plants and raw ABP arriving at one rendering plant visited. Based on this, only 4% (90 out of 2360) of the remaining consignments of ABP/DP traded to the Czech Republic in 2013 were confirmed in TRACES. Data extracted from TRACES show that in the first nine months of 2014, the situation had improved as 33% (1260 out of 3680) of consignments arriving in the Czech Republic were checked. Nevertheless, as the majority of consignments are not notified, the requirements of Article 48(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 are not met.

SVA representatives stated that they are not in a position to comply fully with the requirements of Article 48(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 as to do so would place a considerable administrative burden on the official services and require additional resources, especially in those plants which receive many consignments. Moreover, SVA considered it would be more appropriate that operators should confirm the arrival of consignments in TRACES and that risk-based checks that this had been done could be carried out during official controls. The officials met in the regional offices and plants visited supported the SVA position that the need to confirm the arrival of all consignments of ABP/DP as required by Article 48 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 placed an undue administrative burden on them.

responses.response: of SVA: Information from the DG(SANCO) mission, as well as the is findings/conclusions of the FVO inspectors concerning the requirements of Article 48(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009, were communicated and subsequently discussed within the meeting with the RVA representatives held on 12 November 2014. The RVA inspectors were notified of the duty to confirm the arrival of each consignment to the place of destination in the Czech Republic when information of its dispatch was entered in the TRACES system at the place of dispatch in another Member State. Furthermore, they were informed of correct completion of commercial documents by establishment operators ­ both national for the Czech Republic, and harmonised for the trade with the EU Member States. It was emphasized that a paper trader cannot be indicated as the place of destination instead of an approved or registered establishment listed in the list of approved establishments where the ABP/DP can be physically kept/stored (store, processing plant, etc.) of the relevant EU Member State. In the second case the quantities of additives used were not recorded and therefore the maximum limits could not be verified; labelling: out of twelve samples eight were identified with non-conformities (ingredients were missing, including one allergen, format of the batch number was incorrect, one batch number was found illegible, labels missing on some pieces of rabbit meat due to peeling off, label in the Czech language was partially covered on one product and labels did not or not correctly mention some additives); additives: three products were chosen for which additives were not used. Out of the remaining nine samples the CA had findings for four (some specifications were missing, incomplete or out of date, some additives for which the carry-over principle applies were not taken into account by the FBO).

The FVO audit team examined the documentation of these 12 cases. The outcome of this exercise was as follows: tracing (one step backward ­ one step forward): In three cases, the CA did not observe that links were missing, this was particularly the case when traders were involved. In another case the CA did not complete the evaluation. The FVO audit 8 team confirmed the other CA findings. However, the CA considered some retail outlets and the distribution centres used by them as a single food business, even though the locations have different registration/approval requirements and are physically located on different sites. The CA stated that consequently there was no need to ensure traceability for physical movement of products. References for the products, which were not mentioned on the commercial documents were subsequently provided by email by the FBO and were found to be satisfactory by the CAFIA. On the other hand examples were seen where the retail outlets shared IT systems with the suppliers and these systems provided the relevant information requested by Regulation (EU) No 931/2011; available documentation to verify the physical flow of the products within the establishments such as production data for reconciliation, the product recipes, the technical specifications of the additives used: the FVO audit team confirmed the CA finding in all but one case, where the CA did not complete its evaluation; labelling: the FVO audit team confirmed the CA findings based on the documentation provided. For one sample (imported rabbit meat), the absence of labels had been identified during previous SVA inspections at destination in early 2015. The SVA had requested the FBO to take appropriate corrective actions. The SVA stated that the sample taken formed part of the same consignment and the labels were missing due to peeling-off; additives: the FVO audit team confirmed the CA findings based on the documentation seen.

The FVO audit team selected 3 of the 12 cases for on-the-spot verification of the data provided by the CA. The additional findings of this exercise were as follows: tracing (one step backward ­ one step forward) was not satisfactory in one of the three cases: commercial documents for supplied meat did not mention references for batch or lot identification, which is not in line with the requirements laid down in Regulation (EU) No 931/2011. Commercial documents for dispatched composite products containing meat products did not include a reference number. For the two other cases, the FVO audit team confirmed the CA evaluation; reconciliation of the quantities of meat and products thereof and other ingredients used versus the products produced: in one case there was a discrepancy between the labelling and the recipe regarding the amount of meat, fried onion and parsley. The quantities of meat and other ingredients used were not recorded and reconciliation of meat and other ingredients was not possible. Despite the FBO having an internal quality scheme in place, these deficiencies remained unidentified. For the other two cases, the FVO audit team confirmed the CA evaluation; in one out of the three cases, the FVO audit team confirmed the evaluation of the labelling carried out by the CA. For the two other cases, the food labelling was not compliant: for one meat product the label did not specify that it was a smoked product (non-smoked varieties of this product are marketed); for a second meat 9 product, E412 (guan gum) was incorrectly specified on the label as a stabiliser, rather than a thickener; in addition the FVO audit team identified that the official veterinarian and the FBO of one establishment visited calculated the input of nitrite (E250) based on the amount specified in the recipe and not on the actual quantity of meat used in the production1.

Notwithstanding the non-compliance identified, official controls have, during this audit, been generally effective in enforcing the requirement to be able to trace meat and products thereof along the production chain ("one step backwards ­ one step forwards").

Control of incoming goods. In several establishments visited, the FBOs did not ensure that all mandatory information on food supplied was available. Examples were seen where the date of dispatch and/or a reference identifying the lot, batch or consignment and/or the address of the consignee were missing, which is not compliant with the provisions of Regulation (EU) No 931/2011. In one establishment the description of the game meat received was incomplete: the documents did not mention that the products were frozen. This was identified by the official veterinarian. In addition there was a discrepancy between the descriptions of the game meat on the checklist on arrival of game meat against the internal document of acceptance, mentioning 75% and 65% respectively (lean meat%/fat). The delivery documents did not mention the meat/fat content. In the same establishment, fresh meat was received from an establishment approved for cutting only2, whilst the meat was processed. The delivery document mentioned frozen pork trimmings 85/15. The SVA investigated this case and confirmed at the final meeting that it concerned minced meat (trimmings mixed with fat in the mincer) instead of trimmings. In another establishment the FBO had a procedure for recording incoming meat. For one consignment verified, bone-in meat received was recorded as boneless meat, thus making the quantity of meat appear greater than that actually received. In one game handling establishment, wild game was received from different wild game collection centres of which one was not registered in the SVA database. From this collection centre one stag was collected which arrived at the game 2 In their response to the draft report the CA noted that: "the establishment has been approved for cutting, storing, processing, transporting and selling to the final consumer since 12 May 2010. Routine CA controls are effective in identifying most deficiencies relating to traceability (one step backwards ­ one step forwards) but failed to detect some systemic non- compliances in some establishments.

citations.text: According to the data provided by CAFIA, the number of registered primary producers has increased from 1 281 in 2012 to 2 019 in May 2015. The CA explained that the reason for this increase is mainly due to the fact that since CAFIA was delegated to conduct inspections on behalf of the payment agency for Cross Compliance (CC), more FBOs have become known to CAFIA. In relation to primary production, the registration database contains details whether the FBO is dealing with fruit and/or vegetables, but there is no information available on the specific crop being grown which precludes the possibility of planning official controls on an appropriate risk basis as required by the Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 6

There is a system in place for registration of food establishments. However, the lack of information on the crops grown by primary producers weakens the effectiveness of the risk based planning of official controls as required by Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

CAFIA informed the FVO audit team that primary production sectors are included in the scope of the current risk assessment for inspections. However, individual primary producers are currently not entered in the database that is used for the selection of FBOs to be audited. Consequently primary producers have not been subject to risk based controls at the time of the audit as required by Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. The CA informed the FVO audit team that the database would be adapted in June 2015. The regional inspectorates of CAFIA are responsible for planning of "ad hoc" inspections to primary producers. The FVO audit team was informed that the same principles for the risk assessment are applied by the Regional Inspectorates. However, it was noted that the current registration system for primary producers does not include either information regarding actual crops grown by the growers or information related to private certification schemes the grower may be adhered to. After an inspection takes place, information related to these aspects is recorded for future planning.

In one of the Regional Inspectorates visited during the audit, roughly 400 FBOs were registered for primary production and 6 so-called comprehensive inspections were conducted in 2014. The crops involved were combinable crops, sugar beet and potato. Additionally two inspections were conducted in 2014 based on consumer complaints related to crops like garlic, onion, potatoes and apples. The comprehensive inspections were not targeting high priority crops identified by the EFSA Opinions on the matter.

CISTA informed the FVO audit team that the inspections conducted at growers were under three different inspection frameworks, CC, Delegated Inspections and National Controls. The inspections conducted for CC and National Control schemes control contamination arising from fertilisers (as defined within Annex I Part A, II, point 3 (a) of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004) such as the use of manure and sewage sludge which is banned for use in soil where vegetables and fruits are grown. The inspections for CC were planned to reach 1% of the registered growers and for National Controls between 400 and 500 inspections were conducted each year. However, the CISTA representative stated that the risk assessments for the planning of such inspections do not take into consideration the microbiological contamination to target the producers and/or crops to be inspected. 9

citations.text: The audit team noted that, when developing the audit programme, SVA has not properly defined all relevant audit areas (the audit areas are not sufficiently detailed e.g. animal health is determined as an audit area although this could be further broken down to different animal species, activities, diseases etc.) and the audit programme development process is not well-documented as regards risk-based prioritisation (it is not evident whether all relevant areas were considered and on which basis decision on selection of audit topics was made).

The audit areas in CAFIA audit system are expanded since 2011, and the annual audit programme indicates an addition of new audit topics. The topics include microbiological sampling, traceability, genetically modified organisms in food, risk-based planning of official controls etc. The audit team noted that there is no evidence on how new topics are determined and there is no overview of the areas that need to be considered in the audit programme. In addition, there is no evidence that the development of the audit programme has considered all relevant areas, and it is not evident how this results in risk based prioritisation and effective coverage of all areas in a reasonable timeframe.

The audit team noted that CISTA has not adequately defined the areas that need to be covered by the audit activities. In addition although the planned arrangements refer to risk based planning of audit programmes, CISTA could not demonstrate that audit programmes resulted from a risk-based prioritisation.

All three CCAs have developed and implemented processes for establishing annual and multiannual audit programmes. These processes are not adequately documented thus the CCAs cannot demonstrate that all relevant areas have been considered, an adequate coverage in a reasonable timeframe has been achieved and that audit programmes result from a risk-based prioritisation.

The audit team noted that those assessments cover the internal audit functions within the context of the relevant requirements of the ISO standard.

There is no particular focus (in the external assessment done to date) on the audit process to ensure that the process is capable of producing objective results and meeting its obligations under Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 (e.g. no assessment of the risk-based planning and of the independence of the audit process and auditors, no opinion on effectiveness of the audit process etc). The audit team considered that the CCAs have inadequate arrangements in place to fulfil the requirement of Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 as regards the independent scrutiny of the audit process. 9 Conclusions

All CCAs have arrangements in place to ensure independent scrutiny of their quality management systems through the ISO certification external audits that they receive. However, those arrangements do not sufficiently cover the audit processes contrary to the requirements of Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 5.2.3 Auditor competence 5.2.3.1 Legal requirements Articles 2(6) and 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 do not lay down specific requirements regarding the competence of auditors. Article 6 of the same Regulation requires that staff performing official controls "receive, for their area of competence, appropriate training enabling them to undertake their duties competently" and "keep up-to-date in their area of competence and receive regular additional training as necessary" Section 6.6 of the Annex of Commission Decision 2006/677 provides guidance on auditor competence: "Auditor competence and selection criteria should be defined under the following headings: -- generic knowledge and skills -- audit principles, procedures and techniques; management/organisational skills, -- specific technical knowledge and skills, -- personal attributes, -- education, -- work experience, -- auditor training and experience. It is essential to put a mechanism in place to ensure auditors are consistent and their competencies are maintained. Competencies required by audit teams will vary depending on the area they are auditing within the control or supervision systems. As regards the technical knowledge and skills required by auditors, the training requirements for staff performing official controls (Chapter 1 of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 882/2004) should also be considered." 5.2.3.2 Findings

recommendations.text: To ensure that, as required by Article 8(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, documented procedures: are adequately followed by all RVAs so that travelling and resting times in proposed journey plans are adequately assessed until the final place of destination in the non-EU country; correctly reflect the requirement of Article 14(1)(a)(i) of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005 that certificates of competence of all drivers and attendants involved in the journey must be verified by the competent authority at the place of departure.

citations.text: A few shortcomings in the methodological guidelines were noted such as the request that only one driver's certificate of competence was required and checked for approved journey plans that would require two drivers. The audit team saw several examples of the RVAs implementing these controls as set out in the methodological guidance.

The audit team found the methodological guidance to be generally aligned to the relevant legal requirements. A shortcoming was noted resulting in checks in driver's certificate of competence being insufficient, as only one driver was checked instead of the two required, for the approved long distance journeys. This shortcoming undermines the assurances necessary for the protection of animals during transport.

The RVAs systematically check organisers' plans to rest the animals during the journey and provide them with feed and water (Article 14 of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005): In April 2017 the SVA issued an instruction that the journey plan has to be until the final place of destination in the non-EU country, as indicated by the Zuchtvieh judgement1. The audit team noted that in one of the regions visited the stamped journey plans extended only until the exit point from the EU, and that local officials were unaware of such a requirement; In the other region visited, the journey plans were until the final place of destination. When assessing these journey plans the RVA officials rightly took into account the amount of time needed to clear Turkish official controls at the border (6 hours). Nevertheless, they were only partially aware of the limited opening hours operated by the Turkish veterinary authorities. This had resulted in stamped journey logs that were unrealistic and that would therefore exceed maximum permitted travelling times before reaching the final place of destination. In March 2017 the SVA issued instructions that a copy of confirmation of the booking of the control post in Svilengrad must be systematically requested. This is a good practice. The RVAs have gone beyond these instructions and are requesting a copy of confirmation of the booking of any control post.

There is a system in place to systematically assess planned and actual resting and travelling times before and after the journey. This system is nevertheless weakened by the failure to ensure that all journey plans always cover the full journey until the final place of destination, in contradiction to the methodological guidance, and that approved journey plans are realistic and achievable as working hours at the Turkish border inspection post are not being taken into account. There is therefore the risk that travelling times are exceeded once past the EU border.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the opening hours of the Turkish border inspection post are taken into account when assessing planned journey logs and carrying out retrospective checks to verify compliance with travelling and resting times, as required by Articles 14(1)(a)(ii) and 15(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005.

recommendations.text: To put in place practical arrangements to increase the number of dead pigs reported and tested for ASF from all registered and non-registered pig holdings (other than in Part I and Part II). ASF Strategy for the Eastern Part of the EU.

citations.text: Between June 2017 and February 2018, 373 and 109 domestic pigs were tested in Part II under active and passive surveillance respectively. In Part I, 129 and 255 pigs were tested under active and passive surveillance respectively. In the remainder of the country, only 5 pigs were tested for ASF under passive surveillance during the same period (see Annex 2). This is not in accordance with the ASF Strategy for Eastern part of EU which recommends enhanced passive surveillance in the whole country.

Although not all home slaughter in Part II receives official inspection, surveillance arrangements for domestic pigs in this area should make early detection of ASF possible. Outside the infected area, passive surveillance for early detection of ASF in domestic pigs is weakened by the fact very few samples are tested. This will hamper the early detection of ASF in this population should it occur.

responses.response: In case of occurrence of avian influenza in the Czech Republic, an online form will be available on the website of the State Veterinary Administration (SVA) to create a census of all commercial and non-commercial holdings in restricted zones. It is a much faster system than the previous paper-based procedure. Municipal authorities are responsible for ensuring performing of emergency veterinary measures in their territory according to the Veterinary Act and i.e. for drawing up the census of holdings. All big mmercial holdings in protection zones will be visited by RVA for clinical examination and laboratory sampling. A number of non-commercial holdings in protection zones is usually very high (over 1000 non-commercial holdings in one protection zone). The SVA does not have the personnel capacity to visit all of non- commercial holdings and to perform audits or on the-spot checks of municipal authorities. citations.text: The audit team noted non-compliances in the abovementioned slaughterhouse related to PMI. The birds fallen from the line before PMI, are not presented for PMI as required in point 1, Part B, Chapter V, Section IV of Annex 1 to Regulation (EC) No 854/2004, but are disposed as unfit for human consumption. Furthermore, all carcases are washed after evisceration before entering PMI (the same non-compliance was detected by the audit team also in another slaughterhouse visited). These non-compliances related to PMI were not noted by the OVs or by the RVA inspectors during their audits.

However, the level of detection by officials of certain non-compliances in the operation of establishments was low. This mainly concerned carcase washing after evisceration 7 and before PMI (see 5.5), discarding fallen carcases before PMI, production hygiene and maintenance of the cold chain, consequently leading to a situation where corrective measures are not taken or imposed.

The audit team noted in two out of three slaughterhouses visited that washing of carcases takes place after evisceration and before PMI. This non-compliance was not detected by any level of CAs. This is a repeated finding from the audit carried out in 2010 when measures were not taken during slaughter to prevent contamination of meat, in particular, the spillage of digestive tract contents during evisceration, as required in point 5, Chapter IV, Section II of Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004.

As the poultry carcases are washed beforehand, PMI of the slaughtered birds cannot be performed as required in point 6, Chapter IV, Section II of Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004. This prevents the officials from taking the appropriate decision concerning meat. Under EU legislation, meat showing signs of faecal contamination shall be declared unfit for human consumption (see point 1(s), Chapter V, Section II of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 854/2004). 10 Conclusions on contamination of carcases

Washing carcases undermines slaughter hygiene and prevents official staff from a) rejecting carcases showing faecal contamination during PMI, and b) from notifying and requiring the operator to take the necessary corrective measures, in order to safeguard food safety and hygiene of production. Therefore, Recommendation No 5 has in practice not been addressed effectively.

citations.text: The OVs met, in general, are capable of detecting deficiencies and are aware of legal requirements. Nonetheless, the audit team noted certain non-compliances during the on- site visits not detected and / or recorded by the officials.

In one slaughterhouse visited, the audit team noticed non-compliances related to stunning (level of water in electrical water bath did not allow immersion of the birds up to the base of the wings) which was not noted by the OV during a daily control. In addition, when the FBO staff demonstrated the check on stunning, the person took a bird from the line after stunning and explained that the bird should wake up in 90 seconds. When the person was advised to check e.g. cornea reflex by the audit team, the person did not perform the check correctly. The OV did not correct the person and explained later that the person was not the animal welfare officer.

The audit team noted non-compliances in the abovementioned slaughterhouse related to PMI. The birds fallen from the line before PMI, are not presented for PMI as required in point 1, Part B, Chapter V, Section IV of Annex 1 to Regulation (EC) No 854/2004, but are disposed as unfit for human consumption. Furthermore, all carcases are washed after evisceration before entering PMI (the same non-compliance was detected by the audit team also in another slaughterhouse visited). These non-compliances related to PMI were not noted by the OVs or by the RVA inspectors during their audits.

The audit team noted in the same establishment that, due to current reconstruction works on that day, the cutting room has no hand-washing facilities. FBO explained that the cutting room is being reconstructed due to the age of the facilities and increased slaughtering capacity. Therefore, personal hygiene is organised in other ways and the OV was aware of this exceptional procedure. The audit team noted in the cutting room 5 that knife disinfection is done by using alcohol spray, in accordance with the FBO's HACCP plan. Washing instructions of knives before disinfection are not included in the plan. The official staff had not noted/recorded this deficiency. During the visit, the hand washing facility in the packing room of fresh poultry meat had no running water. The FBO took immediate action to correct this.

The audit team reviewed some OV records of temperatures of the cold storage rooms in the same slaughterhouse. The audit team saw evidence that the OV had detected a deficiency in cold chain in one freezer (temperatures between -9,6 and -11,9 for five hours as the minimum should be -18) and had informed the FBO. The FBO had explained to the OV that air temperature in this freezer fluctuates when the door is open. The OV had not recorded this non-compliance in a logbook and therefore, there was no evidence if any corrective action had been requested and / or taken.

In the abovementioned slaughterhouse, the inspection frequency is six times per year (the baseline frequency). However, the audit team saw deficiencies in hygiene (as listed above but also due to ongoing reconstruction) that might indicate higher risk and therefore should result in increased inspection frequency.

However, the level of detection by officials of certain non-compliances in the operation of establishments was low. This mainly concerned carcase washing after evisceration 7 and before PMI (see 5.5), discarding fallen carcases before PMI, production hygiene and maintenance of the cold chain, consequently leading to a situation where corrective measures are not taken or imposed.

The audit team noted in two out of three slaughterhouses visited that washing of carcases takes place after evisceration and before PMI. This non-compliance was not detected by any level of CAs. This is a repeated finding from the audit carried out in 2010 when measures were not taken during slaughter to prevent contamination of meat, in particular, the spillage of digestive tract contents during evisceration, as required in point 5, Chapter IV, Section II of Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004.

Washing carcases undermines slaughter hygiene and prevents official staff from a) rejecting carcases showing faecal contamination during PMI, and b) from notifying and requiring the operator to take the necessary corrective measures, in order to safeguard food safety and hygiene of production. Therefore, Recommendation No 5 has in practice not been addressed effectively.

In general, the establishments visited comply with EU requirements or the corrective actions have been taken and are in place to reach the adequate compliance level. The control procedures are adopted by officials. Nonetheless, the audit team detected during the on-site visits certain non-compliances which are described in detail in chapter 5.2. 11

The audit team noted in one slaughterhouse visited that the premises need reconstruction due to the age of the building and the increased production capacity. The audit team saw the FBO's reconstruction plan and some of those planned changes had started by the time of the audit. In another slaughterhouse, speed of the slaughter line in relation to the capacity of chilling and cutting of carcases had a negative impact on progression of cutting and maintenance of the required temperature in meat (the same non-compliance was noted during 2010 audit). Conclusions on FBO's compliance with EU hygiene requirements

Recommendation No 6 is only partially addressed. The corrective actions taken by the CA have not been sufficiently effective to ensure that all deficiencies recorded in the 2010 audit report are corrected, such as issues regarding temperature of meat during cutting. In addition, the official control system in place is not sufficiently responsive, in particular, to new deficiencies related to increased slaughter and production speeds which require reconstruction of the facilities and increased capacity for chilling and cutting carcases to ensure progression of cutting and, consequently, maintenance of the required temperature of the meat.

The audit team noted in the same establishment that, due to current reconstruction works on that day, the cutting room has no hand-washing facilities. FBO explained that the cutting room is being reconstructed due to the age of the facilities and increased slaughtering capacity. Therefore, personal hygiene is organised in other ways and the OV was aware of this exceptional procedure. The audit team noted in the cutting room 5 that knife disinfection is done by using alcohol spray, in accordance with the FBO's HACCP plan. Washing instructions of knives before disinfection are not included in the plan. The official staff had not noted/recorded this deficiency. During the visit, the hand washing facility in the packing room of fresh poultry meat had no running water. The FBO took immediate action to correct this.

The audit team reviewed some OV records of temperatures of the cold storage rooms in the same slaughterhouse. The audit team saw evidence that the OV had detected a deficiency in cold chain in one freezer (temperatures between -9,6 and -11,9 for five hours as the minimum should be -18) and had informed the FBO. The FBO had explained to the OV that air temperature in this freezer fluctuates when the door is open. The OV had not recorded this non-compliance in a logbook and therefore, there was no evidence if any corrective action had been requested and / or taken.

In 2018 the same FBO had carried out a validation of the temperature and time limits for meat in cutting room and based on the results, provided a procedure setting a temperature for meat in cutting room of up to +6,5 maximum for two hours in an ambient temperature of +12. The RVA audit report in 2018 does not mention any non- compliance related to temperature of meat, nor an assessment of the validation. The official staff have records of meat temperatures in the cutting room over + 4 but below 6 +6,5. However, the audit team noted during the on-site visit fluctuation of temperature of meat of over +4 while cutting and wrapping/packaging, up to +8,6. This is not in line with the FBO's own procedures or with EU legislation, which does not provide an for an exemption of a validation which allows the meat temperature to rise up to +6,5 for two hours during cutting.

However, the level of detection by officials of certain non-compliances in the operation of establishments was low. This mainly concerned carcase washing after evisceration 7 and before PMI (see 5.5), discarding fallen carcases before PMI, production hygiene and maintenance of the cold chain, consequently leading to a situation where corrective measures are not taken or imposed.

The audit team noted in two out of three slaughterhouses visited that washing of carcases takes place after evisceration and before PMI. This non-compliance was not detected by any level of CAs. This is a repeated finding from the audit carried out in 2010 when measures were not taken during slaughter to prevent contamination of meat, in particular, the spillage of digestive tract contents during evisceration, as required in point 5, Chapter IV, Section II of Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004.

Washing carcases undermines slaughter hygiene and prevents official staff from a) rejecting carcases showing faecal contamination during PMI, and b) from notifying and requiring the operator to take the necessary corrective measures, in order to safeguard food safety and hygiene of production. Therefore, Recommendation No 5 has in practice not been addressed effectively.

recommendations.text: The competent authorities should ensure that the prioritisation of controls and allocation of resources for animal welfare reflect the objectives of the Multi-annual National Control Plan (MANCP) as required in Article 110(2)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The setting of strategic and operational objectives should take into consideration the guidance provided in the MANCP network reference document "Developing Objectives and Indicators" developed by the MANCP network.

citations.text: The Czech Multi-Annual National Control Plan (MANCP) (2016-2018 - latest version), section 3.3, Strategic Objectives, includes a policy objective relevant for animal welfare: Objective two: "Ensure a high level of protection of human and consumer interests, animal health, animal welfare and plant health." There is no further description of what the SVA considers a high level of protection or how this should be measured.

The first operational objective of the MANCP related to on farm controls aims to ensure the keeping of farm animals in accordance with the minimal requirements - ensuring compliance with the requirements of the national and EU legislation.

The second operational objective of the MANCP focuses on raising awareness about the activities and powers of the competent authorities; responsibilities of breeders and general public involvement. A third aims for more effective procedures and enhanced cooperation between competent authorities: SVA, Regional Veterinary Authorities (RVAs) and Municipalities with extended powers (those that are legally entitled to enforce and sanction legislative requirements for farm welfare laws).

As the first MANCP operational objective on farm welfare solely reflects basic monitoring of compliance, there is no link between the planned prioritisation of controls and the allocation of resources to reflect strategic objective two of the MANCP described in paragraph 1 of this report or any of the operational objectives described in paragraphs 2 and 3 of this report. This is not in line with article 110 (2) (a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 that requires the prioritisation of controls and allocation of resources to reflect the strategic objectives of the MANCP.

There are no baselines set to measure if outcomes for animal welfare meet strategic or operational objectives. For example, the SVA has been monitoring post-mortem indicators in broiler slaughterhouses from each production unit (flock and house) since 2011. From 2013 this data was used to target the poorest performing farms and from 2017 it started including also the incidence of footpad dermatitis (FPD). According to the SVA thresholds, the data indicate unsatisfactory scores for lesions of approximately 75% of flocks sent to slaughter in 2017, 2018 and 2019. The SVA had access to full data from the end of 2018. The use of the indicators to target inspections has had no impact on the outcome of compliance levels since the end of 2017, which remains unchanged (as farms inspected continued to register unsatisfactory scores). Thus, the SVA carries out controls but sets no targets for ensuring compliance with its minimum requirements, nor has it adapted policy objectives to address the situation found from its own monitoring.

There are no specific, measureable strategic or operational objectives or targets indicated in the MANCP on what the Czech Republic wants to achieve for animal welfare outcomes. Examples could include: reduce incidence of tail docking by x%; reduce FPD levels by x%; decrease lameness levels in cattle by x% through official controls and related actions. These could include targeted training for poorly performing sectors, 3 targeted enforcement campaigns on certain issues or; liaison with the relevant sector to set agreed targets for improvement, etc.

The Competent Authorities' approach to the setting of objectives in the MANCP is mainly operational with no defined targets, indicators or measurement of progress and, as such, they are insufficient to bring about measureable change.
There is a good well-developed prioritisation of controls and allocation of resources even though these do not link to clear objectives or targets in the MANCP or annual inspection plans.

Planning of cross compliance and animal welfare controls are well formulated on a demonstrable risk profiling basis using a range of risk criteria that target official resources to inspecting the potentially worst offenders. However, the introduction of post-mortem indicators as a risk criterion to target broiler farm inspections has had no impact on improving animal welfare outcomes for footpad dermatitis over a three- year period.

recommendations.text: The competent authorities should ensure that, in accordance with the requirements of Article 5 and Article 12(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, they shall: 1 (a) have procedures and/or arrangements in place to ensure the effectiveness and appropriateness of official controls and other official activities; and (b) have procedures and/or arrangements in place to ensure the impartiality, quality and consistency of official controls and other official activities at all levels; and 2) Competent authorities shall perform official controls in accordance with documented procedures, and that those procedures shall cover the subject areas for control procedures set out in Chapter II of Annex II and shall contain instructions for staff performing official controls.

citations.text: There are no official control procedures for animal welfare controls on pig or broiler farms. There are no procedures for assessing documentation accompanying broiler flocks to slaughter. There is some specific guidance on measuring microclimate on broiler farms and a specific instruction on the assessment of FPD and a requirement to follow up on unsatisfactory scores. The SVA has made available information documents relating to tail docking of pigs but these are not procedures for official controls. The SVA considers that inspectors should base their assessment primarily on legislative requirements. Although the SVA has given training and held meetings with RVAs, it provided no further documentation to them to ensure they carry out inspections in a comprehensive and consistent manner. Inspectors met indicated that the templates and guidelines for reporting and evaluation of non-compliances for cross compliance inspections ensured consistency and transparency of implementation in this area.

The lack of procedures described in paragraph 13 is not in compliance with 1) Article 5 and 2) Article 12 (1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 which require that: 1) Competent authorities... shall: (a) have procedures and/or arrangements in place to ensure the effectiveness and appropriateness of official controls and other official activities; and (b) have procedures and/or arrangements in place to ensure the impartiality, quality and consistency of official controls and other official activities at all levels; and 2) Competent authorities shall perform official controls in accordance with documented procedures, and that those procedures shall cover the subject areas for control procedures set out in Chapter II of Annex II and shall contain instructions for staff performing official controls.

The Methodology does not provide mandatory compliance criteria. Although farmers are taking some actions, it is insufficient to comply with the legal requirements relating 5 to risks for tail biting. The lack of binding criteria and detailed procedures for inspectors does not enable them to reliably, and consistently, address the legal requirements relating to risks for tail biting and the effectiveness of improvement measures. As a result inspectors cannot effectively enforce Point 8 of Annex I, Chapter I to Council Directive 2008/120/EC as to whether the mutilation should have been carried out in the first place.

For example: the pig premises visited was part of a larger group structure and fattened tail docked pigs received from its breeding premises. Tail biting on the fattening farm was extremely low (0.08%). The company carried out a trial of rearing pigs with intact tails in one batch on one of the four breeding farm locations in the group. This resulted in poor production results and increased tail biting compared to the docked pigs on site. However, the company did not substantially alter farm conditions prior to the trial. They reduced the stocking density by 4.5% and added some basic additional enrichment (sisal ropes) and barley grain to the trial batch. The company veterinarian made an assessment of risk factors for tail docking only after the trial was completed. She drafted a list of recommendations for all of their premises, which addressed the main risk factors, but in a non-specific way: optimise x, improve y etc. However, the group manager undermined the requirements for enrichment material specified by the veterinarian by issuing an instruction to all farm managers following an RVA inspection visit by asking them to ensure all pens had a chain and or a plastic bottle attached to a chain to ensure farms complied with minimum requirements for enrichment material. The Head of the animal welfare department in the RVA of the first region visited viewed these arrangements as satisfactory even though they did not comply with the Methodological guidelines in a number of areas.

The SVA issued new instructions for slaughterhouse OVs on the assessment and scoring of FPD lesions, and the setting, and monitoring of thresholds. However, the procedures do not indicate when to take enforcement action for unsatisfactory results. It requires that "unsatisfactory" FPD scores should be included in the "feedback report" sent to the official services in charge of supervising the farm of origin. This had not been necessary for any flock slaughtered in the slaughterhouse visited in the last 3 years. Nevertheless, national level data showed that broilers from farms within this region had been slaughtered in other regions and had frequently been assessed as "Unsatisfactory". Despite this, no corresponding "Feedback reports" from the other regions had been received in the region where the birds originated in the last 3 years. See also paragraph 5 of this report.

The OV at the slaughterhouse visited did not specifically check the plausibility of cumulative daily mortality rates and accepted the value as declared in the food chain information document. The food chain information document accompanying the poultry to the slaughterhouse always included the cumulative daily mortality rates, in line with legal requirements. The OV at the slaughterhouse stated that although this is not indicated in any procedures for monitoring food chain information, the SVA and RVAs agreed in meetings that if cumulative daily mortality rates exceeded 3% this should be 6 notified by the slaughterhouse OVs to the official services responsible for supervising the farm or origin. There had been one case where the cumulative daily mortality rate was 6.35% but no follow-up action had been recorded for this batch as the farm was on the same site as the slaughterhouse.

The animal welfare fields in the SVA information system for animal welfare checks at the slaughterhouse can indicate "compliant", "not compliant" or "not checked". However, for a number of the parameters evaluated, such as "mortality" (birds dead on arrival), or "fitness and condition of the animal", or "unloading" there is no objective guidance or instruction on how compliance should be assessed. Individual OVs at each slaughterhouse are responsible for deciding what is "compliant" or "non-compliant" and for when they should take enforcement action.

The absence of procedures and templates hinders consistent and effective implementation and enforcement of controls to prevent routine tail docking of pigs and follow up enforcement of unsatisfactory results found during post-mortem inspections of broilers. 7

RVAs used different formats for reporting animal welfare inspections on pig farms in the two regions visited. In the first region, inspectors used a template form with prepopulated areas for inspection findings printed on the form and expanded these with free text when they noted non-compliances. The other region used a free text style that had no standard reporting format, leaving the option to individual inspectors to complete the findings. The lack of standard report templates and procedures for carrying out and reporting on inspections does not ensure consistent implementation of controls, scope of inspections and reporting, and calls into question the consistency of the data reported for farm controls.

The assessment of non-compliances detected during cross-compliance controls gives a clearer picture of animal welfare problems as it gives conclusions on the severity, 10 extent, permanence and recurrence of the non-compliance. The planning of other animal welfare controls could benefit from the use of this methodology.

However, the SVA did not analyse why inspections on pig or calf farms resulted in higher rates of non-compliance than equivalent inspections on holdings for laying hens (18% for pigs and 9% for calves compared to 2-4% for laying hens). There is potentially useful data within this framework but the reporting is not always reliable. For example, the report indicated that there was 100% compliance for the category "mutilations" in pigs. This is not the case as: approximately 99% pigs are routinely tail docked; the incidence of tail biting reported on farm and at slaughter was very low (from the sample reviewed); and only rudimentary efforts are being made in terms of complying with minimum requirements; including risk assessment, improvement measures, and enforcement.

The SVA explained that the inspection plan prioritised pig farms with fattening pigs for inspection. It considers that farms receiving tail-docked piglets are compliant with tail docking provision. However, the requirements of Point 8 of Chapter I of Annex I to Directive 2008/120/EC on the prohibition of routine tail docking apply to all pigs on either breeding or fattening farms. Even fattening farms that receive piglets already tail docked must have evidence that: there was tail biting on the fattening farm; they have taken improvement measures which attempted to improve the situation and attempted rearing full tailed pigs on site not at another farm under different conditions. The Directive calls for a process of continuous improvement to eliminate or reduce the risk of tail biting to enable the rearing of pigs with intact tails. Clearly one trial on a different farm under different conditions does not meet these requirements. 9

Holdings selected for cross compliance inspections on animal welfare are identified using a number of risk criteria including animal-based indicators such as post-mortem lesions in ruminants and numbers of animals sent to rendering plants. The former does not address whether the activities are suitable to reach the strategic and operational objectives and ensure effective operation of the MANCP, even if it does include enforcement action and its results. The latter does not provide measureable, focussed actions to target recurrent non-compliances in specific areas.

The SVA drafted a set of non-binding guidance documents (hereafter the "Methodology") for farmers and officials as part of the Action Plan on tail docking of pigs and sent it to farmers' organisations and RVAs in November 2018. The Methodology included requirements to assess risk factors for tail biting and listed some welfare indicators, both animal and resource based to take into consideration, but they are not mandatory for farmers and cannot be legally enforced by RVAs.

The Methodology does not provide mandatory compliance criteria. Although farmers are taking some actions, it is insufficient to comply with the legal requirements relating 5 to risks for tail biting. The lack of binding criteria and detailed procedures for inspectors does not enable them to reliably, and consistently, address the legal requirements relating to risks for tail biting and the effectiveness of improvement measures. As a result inspectors cannot effectively enforce Point 8 of Annex I, Chapter I to Council Directive 2008/120/EC as to whether the mutilation should have been carried out in the first place.

For example: the pig premises visited was part of a larger group structure and fattened tail docked pigs received from its breeding premises. Tail biting on the fattening farm was extremely low (0.08%). The company carried out a trial of rearing pigs with intact tails in one batch on one of the four breeding farm locations in the group. This resulted in poor production results and increased tail biting compared to the docked pigs on site. However, the company did not substantially alter farm conditions prior to the trial. They reduced the stocking density by 4.5% and added some basic additional enrichment (sisal ropes) and barley grain to the trial batch. The company veterinarian made an assessment of risk factors for tail docking only after the trial was completed. She drafted a list of recommendations for all of their premises, which addressed the main risk factors, but in a non-specific way: optimise x, improve y etc. However, the group manager undermined the requirements for enrichment material specified by the veterinarian by issuing an instruction to all farm managers following an RVA inspection visit by asking them to ensure all pens had a chain and or a plastic bottle attached to a chain to ensure farms complied with minimum requirements for enrichment material. The Head of the animal welfare department in the RVA of the first region visited viewed these arrangements as satisfactory even though they did not comply with the Methodological guidelines in a number of areas.

The absence of procedures and templates hinders consistent and effective implementation and enforcement of controls to prevent routine tail docking of pigs and follow up enforcement of unsatisfactory results found during post-mortem inspections of broilers. 7

The SVA explained that the inspection plan prioritised pig farms with fattening pigs for inspection. It considers that farms receiving tail-docked piglets are compliant with tail docking provision. However, the requirements of Point 8 of Chapter I of Annex I to Directive 2008/120/EC on the prohibition of routine tail docking apply to all pigs on either breeding or fattening farms. Even fattening farms that receive piglets already tail docked must have evidence that: there was tail biting on the fattening farm; they have taken improvement measures which attempted to improve the situation and attempted rearing full tailed pigs on site not at another farm under different conditions. The Directive calls for a process of continuous improvement to eliminate or reduce the risk of tail biting to enable the rearing of pigs with intact tails. Clearly one trial on a different farm under different conditions does not meet these requirements. 9

There was clear evidence of routine tail docking noted in inspection reports but due to the SVA guidance on farms receiving tail docked pigs, or the non-binding nature of the Methodology, inspectors indicated that these farms were compliant.

RVAs used different formats for reporting animal welfare inspections on pig farms in the two regions visited. In the first region, inspectors used a template form with prepopulated areas for inspection findings printed on the form and expanded these with free text when they noted non-compliances. The other region used a free text style that had no standard reporting format, leaving the option to individual inspectors to complete the findings. The lack of standard report templates and procedures for carrying out and reporting on inspections does not ensure consistent implementation of controls, scope of inspections and reporting, and calls into question the consistency of the data reported for farm controls.

The SVA will consider how the above and future QA schemes could complement the system of official controls once they are operational. Regulation (EU) 2017/625 requires competent authorities to consider such schemes as part of the risk basis for performing official controls from 14 December 2019.

The SVA has included a number of animal welfare indicators in its Methodology guidance for farmers and officials (on the prohibition of routine tail docking) but the non-mandatory nature of the document severely limits its effectiveness and impact.

The introduction of requirements in 2019 for the monitoring of docked/undocked pigs and tail injuries at slaughter is a good indicator. This could feed into policy development, and objective setting, if the CA ensures the reliability of the data (calibration of assessment); completes analysis of the data; and uses it effectively, which had not been done for the monitoring of footpad dermatitis. 12

citations.text: The audit team reviewed the approval document of a milk collection centre (MCC). recommendations.text: To ensure, when granting approval for permanent operation of a processing plant in accordance with Article 24(2)(b)(i) of Regulation (EC) 1069/2009, that the plant meets all of the infrastructure and equipment requirements to prevent the risk of cross-contamination.
recommendations.legal_basis: Articles 24(2)(b)(i), 25(3)(a), and 44 of Regulation (EC) 1069/2009, and Point 2, Section 4 of Annex IV to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011.

citations.text: The audit team examined a number of approval files and noted that, with the exception of one processing plant, SVA carried out these approvals in line with the rules for registration and approval laid down in Articles 23, 24 and 44 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. However, in the case of one processing plant, the competent authority granted approval while the audit team noted that it should not have been the case, as: a. the layout of the plant did not comply with requirements applicable to the functioning of a plant processing Category 3 and Category 1 materials in the same premises, and b. neither the operator nor the authority did take into account and addressed the relevant risks to public and animal health associated with handling, processing and storage in the same premises of raw ABP and DP of Category 1 material and Category 3 material. Consequently, there was a direct risk of possible cross-contamination between the Category 3 and the Category 1 material in this plant. The above are not in line with requirements of Articles 24(2)(b)(i) and 25(3)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009, and Point 2 in Section 4 of Annex IV to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011. The audit team clarified that this situation resulted from an incorrect interpretation, by the competent authority, of the applicable requirements. The SVA representative explained that during its operations, the operator had in place some procedures mitigating the risk of cross-contamination; moreover, the entire production of Category 3 DP was destined for production of pet food. SVA presented also evidence that, at the time of this audit, the operator was conducting some infrastructure works on the layout of the plant and installations used for processing. Consequently, SVA would carry out a new approval process.
The registration and approval process implemented by SVA was, with one exception, effective and provides assurance that ABP operators, establishments and plants meet their respective obligations.

citations.text: SVA and CAFIA have put staff training arrangements in place, addressing one of the recommendations from the 2013 audit. Any newly recruited veterinary official in SVA is required to pass an attestation within three years, which includes generic knowledge on legislation, hygiene (including a two hour HACCP module) as well as animal welfare and animal health. SVA and CAFIA also provided examples of the staff participation in the European Commission Better Training for Safer Food programme.

SVA provides compulsory annual training on selected topics and asks staff to choose additional voluntary training from a catalogue of training topics. The training catalogue offered 106 courses in 2019, 112 in 2020 and 128 in 2020. The audit team noted that no specific training in fishery products or HACCP was available in the catalogue.

The Ministry of Agriculture organises online training since 2011, available to SVA and CAFIA officials, which includes module No. 9 on HACCP-based procedures. According to the CA, this module requires about 6 hours of self-study and a final test. This online training was followed by 88 and 79 officials in 2020 and 2021, respectively. 4

The audit team noted a solid HACCP knowledge in the officials performing the FBOs audits. These auditors receive compulsory training on basic HACCP (23 hours) to be lead auditors, and are offered voluntary training on advanced HACCP (15 hours). The audit team also reviewed the HACCP training provided in 2018 and new training sessions scheduled in 2022 and found these satisfactory.

According to SVA statement, within routine inspections, inspectors need basic knowledge about HAACP, as they must assess FBO HACCP basic elements such as layout, critical control points, surveillance records, corrective action taken, etc.

The audit team interviewed SVA inspectors from two RVAs, with different years of experience, taking part in routine inspections, noting that in some cases, inspectors lacked sufficient knowledge of the HACCP principles to perform the assigned tasks. This is not in line with Article 5.4(c) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, in respect of the subject matter included in its Annex II, Chapter I points (5) and (7). Transparency and confidentiality

Training programmes are in place and officials have in general sufficient knowledge and experience to perform official controls. However, the training provided was not sufficient to enable inspectors performing routine inspections to reliably check basic aspects of the FBO's HACCP.

recommendations.text: The competent authority should take the necessary measures to ensure that national legislative provisions concerning cold storage of fishery products are in line with the requirements set out in point 2 Chapter VII, Section VIII, Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004.

citations.text: The audit team found an internal regulation (Order 366/2005 of 5 September 2005 concerning requirements applicable to certain frozen foods) that permits the temperature of frozen fishery products in approved cold storage facilities to fluctuate between -15°C and -18°C when handed during storage. The CA stated that this is an obsolete order which should be amended as soon as possible, and that the above requirement from Regulation (EC) No 853/2004 is consistently applied during controls, so premises are not approved unless they comply with the -18°C requirement. recommendations.text: To ensure that official controls consistently check that feed business operators meet the requirements for hazard identification in their respective hazard analysis and critical control point plans, and that the result is recorded in the report of said controls.
recommendations.legal_basis: Articles 6 and 7 of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005, and Article 13(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: In all of the establishments visited, the audit team scrutinised the most recent inspection reports and interviewed the inspectors on their assessment of the operators' HACCP plans. The audit team noted that the inspectors' assessment of the hazard identification part of the HACCP plan was deficient in several establishments. In general, the hazard identification part of the operators' HACCP plans was generic (e.g., the same hazards were identified for all incoming feed materials and other ingredients with an identical risk score) without the level of detail necessary for a proper hazard identification (as required by Article 6(2)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005) and consequent risk assessment. Moreover, certain relevant hazards were not identified by the operators (e.g., pesticides and genetically modified organisms in feed materials of plant origin, heavy metals in feed additives/premixtures of mineral origin or obtained via chemical synthesis). This issue was not reflected in any of the inspection reports seen and operators were thus unaware that there were deficiencies in their HACCP plans. The audit team noted that, during the interviews, some inspectors correctly identified these deficiencies.

In one feed material producer, the operator used direct drying. In the hazard analysis of this processing step, the assessment of the possible occurrence of dioxins/polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) had not been carried out and, consequently, there were no measures in place to monitor/control that relevant hazard. This omission was overlooked in the records of the previous official controls.

While the planning of inspections is largely based on appropriate risk-related factors and official controls are carried out on all operators on a risk basis and with an appropriate frequency, the effectiveness of controls is weakened by some shortcomings in inspectors' assessment of (i) feed business operators' hazard identifications within their hazard analyses and critical control point plans, and (ii) operators' traceability systems (in particular collection and storage of retained samples). 5.2.2 Sampling and analysis 5.2.2.1 Planning of official sampling

recommendations.text: To ensure that official controls consistently check feed business operators' compliance with legislative requirements concerning the appropriateness of retained samples.
recommendations.legal_basis: part 4 of the section "Quality control" of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005.

citations.text: Routine inspections include a verification of operators' traceability systems, including the operators' obligation to take samples of ingredients and from each batch of products manufactured and placed on the market, or of each specific portion of production (in the case of continuous production) in sufficient quantities, using a procedure pre-established by the manufacturer (hereinafter `retained samples'). This is required in part 4 of the section "Quality control" of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. The audit team scrutinised the operators' documentation on collection, packaging, labelling and storage of retained samples, interviewed the feed inspectors who usually control those establishments and made the following observations: · in several establishments, a significant number of the retained samples were not adequately sealed; · in general, the retained samples were formed after the material had been tested within each operator's own control programme thus the material had been subject to diverse manipulations before being retained; · in one feed material producer, no retained samples were collected (and stored) from liquid feed materials; · in another feed material producer, the retained samples were formed by aggregating material from several consecutive batches manufactured. These observations are not in line with the legal requirements established in part 4 of the section "Quality control" of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005 and were not identified in any of the recent inspection reports seen.

While the planning of inspections is largely based on appropriate risk-related factors and official controls are carried out on all operators on a risk basis and with an appropriate frequency, the effectiveness of controls is weakened by some shortcomings in inspectors' assessment of (i) feed business operators' hazard identifications within their hazard analyses and critical control point plans, and (ii) operators' traceability systems (in particular collection and storage of retained samples). 5.2.2 Sampling and analysis 5.2.2.1 Planning of official sampling

recommendations.text: To ensure that the staff carrying out official sampling apply practices ensuring the legal, and technical validity of the samples taken.
recommendations.legal_basis: part 9.4. of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009.

citations.text: CISTA has prepared guidance on official sampling, including a sampling report template, based on the requirements laid down in Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009. However, the audit team noted that the sizes of aggregate and final samples, established for feed additives and premixtures, were considerably lower than the requirements laid down in parts 6 and 7 of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009. No explanations were given for this discrepancy with the EU legal requirements.

The audit team observed official sampling being conducted in three compound feed manufacturers visited (the matrix and parameters to be controlled were suggested by the audit team). In all of the establishments, the feed inspectors sampled for analytes likely to be non- uniformly distributed in the matrix. The audit team noted that all of the inspectors adequately implemented the pertinent legal requirements, as established in Regulation (EC) No 152/2009. However, during the preparation of the final samples, none of the inspectors used a divider (and did not have one), as required by part 9.4 of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009.

In the visited laboratories, validation documentation for nine analytical methods (e.g., determination of coccidiostats, heavy metals, mycotoxins, vitamins, etc.) was examined by the audit team. For eight of these there was no documented evidence on sufficient characterisation which is not in line with the requirements laid down in Article 34(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The audit team pointed out that, for standardised methods (e.g., those complying with relevant internationally recognised rules or protocols including those of the European Committee for Standardisation (CEN)), such information could be retrieved from the relevant publications.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the procedures used by the official laboratories for the preparation of final samples result in the correct amounts being weighed out in line with the methods of analysis and that said samples are homogeneous.
recommendations.legal_basis: part A.1. of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009.

citations.text: In the visited laboratories, the audit team scrutinised the system of preparation of the final samples submitted for testing. In neither was there documentary evidence that the amounts weighed out, as provided for in the methods of analysis, were homogeneous and representative of the final samples. This is a requirement laid down in part A.1. of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009. In one laboratory, a homogeneity study report for sample preparation of food samples for mycotoxin testing was presented to the audit team. The team identified that complete homogenisation had not been achieved for ochratoxin A, and that aflatoxin B1 (regulated in feed) had not been included in the study.

Notwithstanding the risk-based approach adopted for the planning of official sampling and the fact that the laboratories used for testing are appropriately designated and accredited, shortcomings in the implementation of sampling and especially in the preparation and testing of official feed samples, combined with the absence of reporting the analytical recovery (and use thereof for decision making) undermine the legal and technical validity of the samples and the reliability of decisions made on the basis of the results. citations.text: For the nine analytical methods the audit team examined the internal quality control systems in place and noted that (i) the matrices used for the preparation of fortified (positive) control samples had not been identified in a documented traceable manner and thus were not metrologically traceable, (ii) two commercial reference materials had been used beyond the the validity period established by the supplier without supporting documentation proving unaltered values of the reference materials, and (iii) in one laboratory, there was no system on evaluating the acceptability of the results of multiple parallel runs; there was a system in the second laboratory visited and for LC-MS/MS methods the majority of the results of the parallel runs were consistently rejected by the statistical software due to unacceptable variation between the values.
