recommendations.text: To ensure that, in the event of established non-compliance(s) being identified, the central competent authority puts arrangements in place to ensure the quality and consistency of the actions taken by its regional departments in respect of verification of remediation of the non-compliance(s) by the feed business operator and prevention of further recurrences.

citations.text: Approximately 1% of the official controls identified serious non-compliances (e.g., cross- contamination with coccidiostats/veterinary medicinal products, quality problems with produced feed). The audit team reviewed three feed safety-related non-compliances (all concerns samples taken during routine controls). Whilst the feed inspectors could provide evidence (official reports) that follow-up of these non-compliances had been carried out, the reports did not adequately indicate that the origin and extent of the non-compliance had been determined, or that the competent authority had taken appropriate measures to ensure that the operators had remedied the non-compliances and prevented further occurrences of such non- compliances. This is not in line with the requirements laid down in Article 138(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

The audit team noted that, at the time of the above-mentioned follow-ups and the audit, the central level of CISTA did not have arrangements in place to ensure the quality and consistency of the follow-up investigations carried by its regional departments. This is not in line with the requirements laid down in Article 5(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The CISTA representative explained to the audit team that such a system had existed before COVID and that there is an intention to reactivate its functioning.

The audit team noted that, in another case the FeBO had not been informed by the competent authority about the non-compliance identified through official sampling. This is not in line with the requirements laid down in Article 13(2) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. 10 Conclusion on the actions taken on non-compliances

Notwithstanding the fact that the competent authority took actions when non-compliances had been identified in the course of official controls, the competent authority did not ensure the quality and consistency of official controls in relation to (i) determination of the origin and extent of the non-compliances, (ii) operator remediation of the non-compliance, and (iii) prevention of their further occurrences. Collectively these shortcomings weaken the effectiveness of the system of official controls on feed.

citations.text: It was confirmed that the Czech Agriculture and Food Inspection Authority (CAFIA) cross report MRL exceedances to CISTA and this in turn triggers extraordinary controls on professional users. However, the results of the annual residue monitoring programme are not used to enhance the risk based elements of choosing which professional users to inspect as required by Article 24 (2)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

recommendations.text: Ensure that official controls are carried out without prior notice as required by Article 9 (4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: The official controls are routinely performed with up to two or three days prior notice being given which is in conflict with Article 9 (4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, which requires no prior notice be given before controls are carried out except where particular circumstances require that notice is given. This was further confirmed by the inspectors from the regional departments. However, official controls are carried out in a way that minimises disruption or administrative burden to the entities inspected as required by Article 9 (5) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. 10

Official controls at professional user level with the exception of extraordinary controls, are performed with prior notice, as are the majority of official controls carried out at PPP manufacturing and distribution level, thus taking away from the overall effectiveness of the control programme.

Controls are generally carried out with at least some level of prior notice. This can be as little as twenty-four hours or as much as a few weeks depending on the circumstances. It is more routine that two to three days' notice is given to the entity being inspected which is not coherent the requirement laid down by Article 9(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Importation of PPPs for use in other MSs or third countries

The audit team observed 3 routine controls of professional users of PPPs and all incorporated the use of both control questionnaires mentioned in the preceding paragraphs. Two of the controls involved farming companies and the other control was carried out on a company involved in managing and maintaining private and public spaces. The same main process was used in all three controls by different inspectors. To avoid wasted journeys and wasting time it is routine that controls are announced in advance. This prior notice can be as little as 1 day but is more generally 2-3 days. It was noted that "extraordinary controls" are performed without any prior notice. Professional users are required by law to record their PPP use by the following working day after the application, therefore when a control takes place the professional user should have the most up to date records available at hand. However, it is routine that professional users are afforded some additional time to provide these records to the inspector in electronic form.

recommendations.text: Ensure that lists of legal and natural entities which are subject to official controls are maintained and updated annually to ensure that each entity and each PPP store used by that entity are subject to official control as required by Article 10 (2) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: The CISTA provided the audit team with a comprehensive set of lists which act as a basis for the PPP marketing control programme. It was explained during the course of the audit that the lists do contain some overlaps, which is understandable as some operators may function in multiple ways. However, it is conceivable that a manufacturer, not registered as a professional use PPP distributor will not be automatically inspected annually. They may be picked for inspection each year, but this is dependent on each individual regional department. It is also the case that some of the manufacturers and other operators offer products for sale on-line, but yet do not appear on the "on-line" list. There are lists of distributors, re- packers, manufacturers, importers and online sellers maintained by the DAIC of the CISTA, however, during the course of the audit it was found that in some cases the lists were incomplete or at very least not up to date.

One such example is where the actual full list of premises associated with at least three distributors was not up to date. recommendations.text: To ensure that wines bearing a PGI designation, are also covered by 2. systematic verification that they meet the conditions set out in the product specification, as required by Article 19 (1) and (4) of Regulation (EU) 3. 2019/34. The recommendation is based upon conclusion No 58 To ensure that for the verification of PDO/PGI wines during production and marketing, the inspection plans implemented include specific checklists covering every stage of production for each PDO/PGI wine as required by article 19(3)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2019/34. The recommendation is based upon conclusion No 71 To review the control system in light of the high level of non-compliances identified during the post-market controls and adapt as necessary in order to ensure that a PDO/PGI wine designation will not be used unless the results of official testing confirm that the product complies with the conditions set out in the product specification and possesses all the appropriate characteristics of the designation concerned, in line with point 4(a) of Article 19 of Regulation 2019/34. The recommendation is based upon conclusion No 71

citations.text: The information kept in the database makes possible full traceability of PDO and PGI wines. CAFIA verifies the origin and the quality of PDO wines and issues administrative decisions for the classification and marketing of PDO wines. Such controls are not required for wines intended to be marketed as PGI (see also paragraphs 33, 46 and 66 below). The eligibility for using PDO/PGI designations is also checked when the products are placed on the market, particularly in the retailers' chain.

Operators wishing to market their wine as PDO have to request the classification of every batch of wine produced by CAFIA. This is achieved at the expense of an administrative fee paid to CAFIA, which becomes income of the state budget. The classification procedure is based on the verification of grapes and on analytical and organoleptic testing. The wine classification carried out by CAFIA ensures the traceability of the origin and the quality of every batch of wine intended to be marketed as PDO (e.g. "quality wine" or "quality wine with an attribute"). However, such a system is not in place for PGI wines.

The authenticity of the marketed wines is verified through official analytical testing carried out in the laboratory of CAFIA. The sensory commission of CAFIA carries out organoleptic testing. Where the traceability of sampled wines cannot be otherwise verified, the laboratory is requested to carry out isotopic analysis of wine samples. However, the examination of the authenticity is not an option for PGI wines, as no classification involving at least sampling for analytical testing is carried out for wine batches intended to be marketed as PGI products. Samples of PGI wines taken during production and marketing aim to verify that they meet the general conditions of the relevant product specification.

Although the inspections serve to validate the approval procedure for PDO wines and the organoleptic and analytical testing required by point (a) of first subparagraph of Article 19(1) of Regulation (EU) 2019/34, the batches of domestically produced wines sampled upon suspicion, are not blocked until the results of the testing verify their compliance. This is not in line with point 4(a) of Article 19 of Regulation 2019/34, which requires that a product cannot use the PDO/PGI designation relating to it unless the results of the official organoleptic and analytical testing prove that the product in question complies with the conditions in the product specification and possesses all the appropriate characteristics of the PDO/PGI designation concerned. The consequence is that when the CA detects non-compliant PDO/PGI wines, these might have already been marketed thus not all quantities can be recalled, as noted by the audit team during interviews with CAFIA inspectors. Although for PDO wines this is somewhat mitigated by the classification system, this is not the case for PGI wines. 18

recommendations.text: To ensure that implementation of the general principles of Integrated Pest Management is enforced at farm level. The enforcement should cover the entire range of professional users in agriculture, forestry and landscaping in line with Article 14(4) of Directive 2009/128/EC and be supported by appropriate penalties as required by Article 17 of the same directive.

citations.text: In 2014, CISTA made an initial attempt to assess the implementation of each of the general principles of IPM for field crops by introducing a point-based system. Under this system, failure to reach a minimum required score resulted in penalties. However, the initiative was eventually abandoned due to its administrative burden and the difficulty with enforcing strict rules against the general principles in the SUD. In addition, CISTA also stated that the usefulness of the results produced following this process is questionable.

Building on this experience, the monitoring of the implementation of IPM general principles in Czechia is now carried out through an annual survey of a representative sample of 104 arable crop producers. Since a large proportion of fruit and vine growers voluntarily participate in the integrated crop production system, they are not included in the IPM survey carried out by CISTA. This approach is not in line with Article 14(4) of the SUD stipulating that the MS should ensure that the general principles of the IPM set out in Annex III of the SUD are implemented by all professional users. In addition, this approach does not provide for the penalties required by Article 17 of the SUD (and Article 139 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625) when IPM is inadequately implemented.

The questionnaire used in the annual survey provides a detailed breakdown of the components of the general principles of IPM. The data collected offers insights into soil and fertilisation practices, cultivation strategies, and plant protection methods. Completing the questionnaire is mandatory. Responses indicating non-compliance with the IPM principles do not result in penalisation of the farmers. This approach ensures that the data collected is unbiased. Based on the survey results, it has been estimated that farmers with arable crops implement on average 54% of the detailed breakdown of the IPM general principles. It should be noted that not all IPM elements are necessarily compatible with every crop or cultivation system, e.g. crop rotation is not feasible in perennial tree crops. MoA stated that they are aiming to increase that percentage by 5% as stated in the fourth bullet point in Target IV of the NAP (see also paragraph 12 above).

The Research Institute for Forest Management is responsible for implementing IPM in forestry. IPM implementation for non-agricultural uses does not fall under the competence of CISTA and is therefore not included in the survey or in any specific scheme, such as those for vineyards and orchards. Conclusions on Integrated Pest Management

For arable crops, the CAs have converted the general principles of IPM into practical and measurable criteria. However, these criteria are not verified during on-farm inspections. Only agricultural practices that relate to specific obligations under certain SMRs and GAECs are verified by inspection. Fruit and vine growers may voluntarily participate in IPM accreditation schemes. Consequently, the enforcement of the general 17 principles of IPM is limited.

recommendations.text: To ensure that a system for gathering information on PPP acute poisoning incidents is put in place in line with Article 7(2) of Directive 2009/128/EC. 21

citations.text: The 2018-2022 evaluation report regarding the implementation of the NAP highlights that in Czechia there is no legally established obligation to report acute or chronic poisoning incidents of persons exposed i.e. to spray drifts. IHIS is the only source of information concerning poisoning associated with hospitalisation. However, incidents are usually registered under a clinical diagnosis and not as poisoning by PPPs. Therefore, it is common to underestimate or not find the actual cause of reported poisoning incident. MoH stated that collecting data on PPP acute and chronic poisoning from the National Register of Occupational Diseases is problematic as the reason that 18 caused the poisoning incident cannot always be established. In addition, poisoning incidents cannot be identified with certainty as caused by a PPP, when the active substance in question has both biocidal and PPP uses.

There is no system in place for gathering information specifically for PPPs acute poisoning incidents and the records available do not distinguish between acute incidents caused by PPPs or biocides. There are no implementing provisions in place to inform persons who might be exposed to PPPs other than those indicated in the PPP labels.
